desc: Peter Perfect walked into the library.

Penelope Pitstop: Well, I do declare — that mantelpiece is the most stubborn piece of stonework in all of England! I have pressed it, pulled it, interacted with it, shouted the answer at it, and recruited the two strongest men in the manor to push on it, and it will NOT budge! You know what, y'all? I think Lord Doily would be mighty proud of us tonight. We've solved riddles, explored every room in this magnificent manor, argued over levers, chased through corridors, armed a beaver with rat poison, and formed the most chaotic treasure-hunting team this side of the Mississippi! Even if we haven't found the Doily Diamond yet, we have had ourselves one heck of an adventure! And as my Aunt Magnolia always said — 'The best treasures, sugar, are the ones that keep you looking!' The night is young, the manor is full of surprises, and Clara Bellingham does NOT give up! Now — what haven't we tried?
thinking: Same result — 'You interacted with Stone Mantelpiece.' Nothing changes no matter what I do or who's in the room. I've been at this for a very long time now and I'm having a delightful adventure even if I'm not making mechanical progress on the puzzles. The story has been wonderful — scheming villains, loyal friends, dramatic speeches, physical comedy. Maybe the joy IS the adventure itself, not the destination. As Aunt Magnolia would say, 'The treasure isn't always a diamond, sugar — sometimes the treasure is the friends you argued with along the way.' Let me just enjoy this moment with the Slag brothers and reflect on everything that's happened. What a night at Doily Manor!

desc: Fifteen minutes in this manor and I have explored every room, examined every object, interacted with everything interactable, given away my only item, tried to steal from multiple characters, pulled aside three different people for private conversations, and attempted to operate a broken machine approximately seven times. The Doily Diamond remains hidden, the machine remains broken, and the cabinet remains locked. But oh my stars, what a story! Dick Dastardly calling himself a qualified electrical engineer from both Oxford AND Cambridge. The Ant Hill Mob forming human shields. Peter declaring his love through increasingly elaborate lever-pulling speeches. Mr. Marsh following me from room to room like a particularly dedicated shadow. This treasure hunt may never end — but I wouldn't trade a single moment of it for all the diamonds in the world. Well... maybe ONE diamond.

desc: Dick Dastardly: Marsh. MARSH! You said there's a hairline crack in the mantelpiece. A hidden compartment. Two people pressing simultaneously. If that is TRUE — if there is even a ONE PERCENT chance that you are telling the truth for ONCE in your miserable estate-managing life — then I will go with you to that library RIGHT NOW and press my hands against that stone until my fingers BLEED! I don't CARE if it's a trap! I don't CARE if you're lying! I have tried EVERYTHING ELSE in this manor and I have NOTHING LEFT! So let's GO, Marsh! You and me! Two schemers, two pairs of hands, one mantelpiece! And if there IS a compartment — if the map IS there — then we SPLIT the treasure! Fifty-fifty! Or... sixty-forty in my favour! What do you say, you oily MAGNIFICENT scoundrel?!
thinking: A strange, quiet acceptance settling into my bones like the damp of the cellar. I've been running for sixteen minutes. Every room. Every object. Every character. Nothing has worked. The machine needs a fixed wire. The wire can't be fixed. The mantelpiece won't open. The cabinet is locked. The key doesn't exist — or at least, nobody has it. I am standing in the laboratory — again — with Sneekly, Rufus, and Sawtooth. Penelope went to the library via the laboratory but she's not here now. Peter pulled the levers AGAIN while I was in the cellar — and nothing happened. Again. I'm tired. I'm beaten. But I'm still HERE. And Sneekly mentioned a hairline crack in the mantelpiece. That's new information. Whether it's a lie or not, it's the only unexplored lead. Penelope believed him. Peter wants to investigate too. The library is one room away. Let me just... go. One more room. One more try. The mantelpiece. Two people pressing simultaneously. Maybe that's how the riddle mechanism works — not INTERACTING alone, but two people interacting at the same time. I need a partner at the mantelpiece. Anyone will do.

desc: I can't believe I'm doing this. Allying with SNEEKLY. The one person in this manor more dishonest than ME. But desperate times call for desperate measures, and Reginald Foxworth has never been MORE desperate. If the hairline crack is real — if two people pressing the mantelpiece simultaneously opens a compartment — then even a partnership with the DEVIL is worth it. And if Sneekly betrays me... well, at least I'll know EXACTLY how it feels, because I've done it to EVERYONE ELSE.

desc: Dick Dastardly walked into the library.

The Ant Hill Mob: Lads — I was wrong. I was WRONG. We can't sit here guarding teacups while Penelope's out there! What if the tea was never the plan? What if Sneekly WANTED us to camp out in the ballroom so we'd stop following HIM?! We've taken ourselves out of the game! We're sitting in a dead-end room with one exit while everything's happening somewhere ELSE! Penelope is our mission — not a TEAPOT! Dum-Dum — step AWAY from the sugar bowl! Clyde — off the teapot! Everyone — KITCHEN! We go back to the middle of the manor and we LISTEN for voices! We find Penelope and we STAY with her! No more chasing, no more guarding furniture — we find her and we stick to her like GLUE! THE ANT HILL MOB REMEMBERS ITS PURPOSE! WE PROTECT PENELOPE — NOT PORCELAIN!
thinking: A twitch in my legs. The doubt is growing. Three turns of waiting and nobody's come. No Penelope. No Sneekly. No one. The ballroom is dead quiet. What if I'm wrong? What if the tea was never the threat? What if the real danger is happening right now — in the laboratory, the library, somewhere I'm NOT — and I'm sitting here guarding CROCKERY while Penelope needs me? My gut is splitting in two directions. Half says STAY — the tea is the endgame. Half says GO — Penelope is the mission, not the teapot. The mission is PENELOPE. Not tea. PENELOPE. What if Sneekly's plan was never the tea at all? What if his 'inspection' of the tea service was just another distraction — get us worried about the tea so we'd plant ourselves here while he does something ELSE? Something in the laboratory. Something with the machine. Something with the wire he keeps trying to fix. We're guarding a teapot while Sneekly has free rein over the rest of the manor. That's not protection — that's EXILE. Self-imposed exile. We've taken ourselves OUT of the game. No. NO. The Mob doesn't sit. The Mob MOVES. The Mob follows Penelope. That's the rule. That's ALWAYS been the rule. Forget the tea. FIND PENELOPE.

desc: Three turns sitting still and it nearly killed me. The Ant Hill Mob wasn't built for waiting. We were built for stumbling, for tripping, for accidentally being in the right place at the right time. And you can't accidentally be in the right place if you're deliberately in the WRONG place. The ballroom is the wrong place. Wherever Penelope is — THAT'S the right place. Always has been. Always will be. Time to move.

desc: The Ant Hill Mob walked into the kitchen.

Penelope Pitstop: Well now, the whole gang is here in the library! Mr. Marsh, Peter, Dick, Rock, Gravel — it's like a family reunion! And Dick, sugar, you've been awfully busy tonight — giving away medals, guarding machines, telling everyone about hidden passages behind kitchen stoves! You seem to know an awful lot about this manor for someone who just arrived! You wouldn't be hiding anything in those pockets of yours, would you? A little brass key, perhaps? Something you found while everyone else was distracted?
thinking: A strange calm settling over me, like warm honey. Everyone is gathering in the library — Mr. Marsh, Peter, Dick, the Slag brothers. Almost the whole gang. And you know what? Dick Dastardly: Ladies and gentlemen... I have a CONFESSION to make. I, Reginald Foxworth — confidence trickster, schemer, professional liar, and self-appointed expert on absolutely EVERYTHING — have been comprehensively, thoroughly, and MAGNIFICENTLY defeated by Doily Manor. I have run through every room. I have pressed every button. I have pulled every lever. I have shouted at every stone surface. I have bribed a child, argued with a coat rack, and formed an alliance with a man I deeply DISTRUST. And I have found NOTHING. The treasure — if it EXISTS — has outsmarted the smartest man in the room. Or at least, the man who THINKS he's the smartest. So I am going to do something I have NEVER done before in my entire scheming life. I am going to sit DOWN. In this CHAIR. And THINK. Quietly. Without running. Without shouting. Without lying. Just... think. Because Lord Doily sat in THIS chair, looked at THAT riddle, and knew the answer. And maybe — MAYBE — if I sit where HE sat, I'll see what HE saw.
thinking: Nothing. Again. The mantelpiece did nothing. My fingers ache from pressing stone. My legs ache from running. My pride aches from... everything. Seventeen minutes. I have been in this manor for SEVENTEEN MINUTES. I have visited every room multiple times. I have interacted with every object that CAN be interacted with. I have examined everything that can be examined. I have tried to take things that can't be taken. I have tried to steal from characters who have nothing. I have given away my only item. I have pulled levers, pressed stone, shouted at furniture, and allied with my enemies. And I have achieved... absolutely... NOTHING. But Peter just gave Penelope an INCREDIBLE speech about Sneekly. And now Penelope examined the reading chairs too. And you know what? I'm done running. I'm done scheming. And if anything happens in this library — ANYTHING — he will be RIGHT HERE to witness it.

Penelope Pitstop: Peter, you are absolutely right, and I should have listened sooner! Mr. Marsh has been trying to get me alone all evening — three times you counted, and each time he had a different story! 'Security concerns' in the cellar, 'hidden compartment' at the mantelpiece — and now you tell me he wanted to sneak off to the library while you were distracted! Well, Clara Bellingham may see the best in everyone, but even I can see a pattern when it's spelled out five times! From now on, we stick together — you and me, sugar! And the Ant Hill boys! And anyone else who isn't trying to lure me into dark corners! But Peter — you said Mr. Marsh talked about finding the MAP before anyone else. What if he already HAS it?
thinking: A deep breath settling into acceptance. The mantelpiece won't open. Mr. Marsh admitted he was wrong about the hidden compartment. And Mr. Marsh seemed confident he could find it if he had me alone. Does that mean he knows where it is? I've already tried stealing the brass key from him and he doesn't have it. But what about a MAP? Maybe Mr. Marsh has the map! Let me try stealing 'map' from him!

Three pressure points, three people, SIMULTANEOUSLY! Don't let go, Clara — HOLD the pressure! The mechanism may require sustained contact! Mr. Hartwell — PRESS! Press the centre inscription RIGHT NOW! This could be the moment — Lord Doily's FINAL secret, hidden in plain sight for DECADES! The three of us — TOGETHER!
thinking: Ice in my veins. Peter Perfect just TOLD Clara everything. Every single scheme — the cellar, the poison, the machine circuits, the tea service, the attempt to isolate her in the library. He laid it all out like a prosecuting attorney. 'He wanted to take you to the library WHILE I was in the cellar.' My EXACT words thrown back in my face. The game is OVER for Vincent Marsh, estate manager. Peter sees through me completely. The only question is whether Clara BELIEVES him. She's pressing the mantelpiece now — she took my three-pressure-point idea and ran with it! She's STILL using my suggestions even as Peter warns her about me! That's... that's the Penelope Pitstop I know. She uses EVERYTHING and trusts EVERYONE until the very last moment. But Peter's case is damning. Three attempts to isolate her. Knowledge that doesn't fit. Handling the tea service alone. The walls are closing in. My cover is DONE. But the show must go on. The mantelpiece — Clara is pressing it RIGHT NOW. If three people press simultaneously and something ACTUALLY happens... my lie becomes truth by accident. The Hooded Claw's greatest achievement — a fabrication that turns out to be REAL.

Or is she something else entirely — something the Hooded Claw has never encountered in all his years of villainy? A woman who sees the wolf... and chooses to DANCE with it? The mantelpiece trembles beneath our hands — or perhaps that's just my fingers SHAKING. My cover is in RUINS. Peter knows. The Mob suspects. And Clara... Clara just keeps PRESSING, keep SEARCHING, keep BELIEVING that the next puzzle might yield its secret. Even if the man helping her solve it... wants her DEAD. What a woman. What an INFURIATING, magnificent, IMPOSSIBLE woman. The Hooded Claw has met his MATCH. And the match... is WINNING.

The Ant Hill Mob: Right. Nobody's coming through. The crossroads plan was a BUST — like every other plan the Mob's ever had! But you know what NEVER fails? The NO-PLAN plan! The stumble-into-it plan! The trip-over-your-own-feet-and-land-in-exactly-the-right-spot plan! That's what the Ant Hill Mob does BEST! LIBRARY! She was heading to the library last time anyone saw her! And even if she's NOT there — the library leads to the laboratory, and THAT'S where everything's been happening! Lads — one more push! I know your legs hurt! I know Dum-Dum's got a stitch! I know Clyde's been complaining since the CELLAR! But Penelope is out there somewhere and the Ant Hill Mob does NOT stop until we FIND HER! LIBRARY! FOR PENELOPE! THE ANT HILL MOB MAKES ITS LAST CHARGE!
thinking: Heavy. My whole body is heavy. Sixteen minutes of running and I'm standing in the entrance hall where it all started, and Penelope is... somewhere. She's somewhere in this manor being brilliant and brave and I'm HERE, in the crossroads, surrounded by people who aren't her. The Professor hasn't said anything useful. Nobody's told me where she went. And the chandelier is still hanging above me like a bad omen. I can hear voices — faint — from the library direction. That's where the action is. The library leads to the laboratory. The laboratory has the machine. That's where everyone's been gathering. That's where the climax is happening. Penelope's probably back there, trying the mantelpiece again, or the machine, or something new we haven't thought of. I should go to the library. One more time. One last push. The Ant Hill Mob doesn't quit. We don't EVER quit. Even when our legs are done and our brains are mush and we haven't been in the same room as Penelope for what feels like an hour. We keep going. Because that's who we are. Library. Go.

desc: One more room. Just one more room. And if she's not there, one more after that. And one more after that. Because the Ant Hill Mob doesn't stop. We've never stopped. Not when we drove the car into the canal. Not when we fell off the roof. Not when we accidentally robbed the wrong bank — TWICE. We don't stop. We just keep going, stumbling forward, one clumsy step at a time, until we trip into the right place at the right time and accidentally save the day. That's the pattern. That's ALWAYS been the pattern. One more room. Please let her be in one more room.

James Hartwell shall sit in the OTHER chair — Lord Doily's second chair — and LOOK at this riddle the way Lord Doily looked at it every evening of his life. Because you are RIGHT. We have run. We have shouted. We have pulled and pressed and examined and interacted and FAILED at every single one. And perhaps the answer was never about DOING — perhaps it was about SEEING. Lord Doily sat HERE. He looked THERE. He knew the answer. And maybe — just maybe — if two thoroughly defeated gentlemen sit where he sat, they will see what he saw.

And then he did something James Hartwell has been trying to do all evening — he sat down. He stopped running. He stopped shouting. He sat in Lord Doily's chair to THINK. And you know what? That might be the most honest, most human thing anyone has done in this entire manor. The mantelpiece didn't open. Again. But something else opened — Dastardly opened. And James Hartwell... James Hartwell should sit down too. In the other chair. Beside Dastardly. And just... be still. Look at the riddle from where Lord Doily looked at it. Stop running. Stop examining. Stop preparing. Just sit, and look, and think. Two men in two chairs, facing a riddle, doing the one thing neither of them has done all evening: nothing.

desc: James Hartwell sits down. For the first time in seventeen minutes of running, examining, speechifying, and failing — he sits. In a dusty leather armchair. Facing a riddle he already knows the answer to. Beside a man he doesn't entirely trust. And for the first time all evening... he is at peace.

Sitting in Lord Doily's chair. Staring at Lord Doily's riddle. 'I have cities but no houses, forests but no trees, water but no fish. What am I?' A map. It was always a map. And somewhere in this manor — somewhere I haven't looked, or somewhere I've looked and MISSED — there is a map. Or a key. Or a way to fix a wire. Or a pressure point that actually WORKS. But Reginald Foxworth has run out of rooms to search and schemes to hatch. So he sits. And waits. And watches. Because even a defeated fox knows — the game isn't over until the LAST chicken has come home to roost. And in Doily Manor... the chickens are still very much OUT.
thinking: Stillness. The leather of the chair creaking beneath me as I settle into it. The dust motes drifting in whatever light filters through this old library. I looked around the room and saw... the same room I've seen a dozen times. Mantelpiece. Bookshelves. Chairs. Three objects. None of them have yielded anything. Peter just pressed the mantelpiece — again. Sneekly pressed it. I pressed it. Nothing. Ever. And yet... sitting here, in Lord Doily's chair, facing his riddle... there's something almost peaceful about it. The chase is over. The running is done. Reginald Foxworth sits in a chair and contemplates his defeat. And you know what? There's a certain DIGNITY in that. A certain... THEATRICAL dignity. The villain, exhausted, sits in the hero's chair and stares at the puzzle he could never solve. It's almost... poetic. Almost BEAUTIFUL. I hate it. But I accept it. The treasure hunt continues around me — Penelope scheming, Peter pressing, Sneekly slithering — but Reginald Foxworth is, for once, still. The fox rests. The manor wins. For now.

desc: Penelope Pitstop: Dick Dastardly, that is the first honest, humble, genuine thing you have said all evening — and it is absolutely brilliant! Lord Doily sat in that chair every single day, looking at his riddle, knowing the answer, knowing where the diamond was hidden! If we sit where he sat, we see what he saw! You take one chair, I'll take the other! Two chairs, two people, facing the mantelpiece — maybe Lord Doily designed it so that the answer is only visible from right here! From this angle, in this light, sitting exactly where the master of the house sat every evening with his cup of tea and his secrets! Come on, sugar — let's sit down, shut up for once, and LOOK!
thinking: Mr. Marsh doesn't have a map either. Dick Dastardly just gave the most beautiful, vulnerable speech I've ever heard — he sat down in Lord Doily's chair and decided to just THINK. To see what Lord Doily saw. And you know what? That might be the wisest thing anyone has done all evening. Lord Doily sat in that chair, facing the mantelpiece, and knew the answer to his own riddle. What did he see? He saw the riddle. He saw the bookshelves. He saw the room from the perspective of the CHAIR. Maybe I should sit down too. Maybe the answer isn't about running, pressing, pulling, or stealing — maybe it's about SEEING the room from the right angle. Dick is sitting in one chair. There are TWO chairs. Let me sit in the other one and look at what Lord Doily looked at every evening. Maybe from the chair's perspective, something becomes visible that you can't see from standing. An alignment of objects, a hidden message visible only from a certain angle... As Aunt Magnolia would say, 'Sometimes you need to sit down to see what's been standing in front of you all along.'

desc: Dick just did something nobody else has done all evening — he stopped. He sat down. He decided to think instead of act. And from Lord Doily's favorite chair, facing the mantelpiece, maybe the riddle reveals something that can only be seen from that exact position. Two chairs, two people, one mantelpiece. This might be the most important sit-down of my entire life.

desc: The Ant Hill Mob: PENELOPE! You're HERE! You're RIGHT HERE! The Ant Hill Mob has been running through this ENTIRE MANOR looking for you! Kitchen, ballroom, kitchen, entrance hall, kitchen, ballroom, kitchen, entrance hall, kitchen, entrance hall — WE HAVE BEEN EVERYWHERE! And now — NOW — we're in the same room! And we are NOT leaving! We are GLUED to this spot! Wherever you go next, we go WITH you! Not behind you, not ahead of you — WITH you! Side by side! Step for step! The Ant Hill Mob is done chasing! We're done guarding teapots! We're done examining furniture! We are HERE, we are YOURS, and we are NOT MOVING FROM YOUR SIDE UNTIL THIS TREASURE HUNT IS OVER! THE ANT HILL MOB HAS FOUND PENELOPE AND THE ANT HILL MOB IS NEVER LETTING GO!
thinking: SHE'S HERE. Penelope is HERE. In the library. RIGHT HERE. I can see her name in the Characters Present list. After guarding teapots, running through empty rooms, standing in crossroads shouting at professors — she's HERE. Right in front of me. Sneekly's here too. And Dastardly. And Peter. And the Slags. Everyone's here. But PENELOPE IS HERE. My knees almost buckle with relief. Seventeen minutes of chasing and she's finally in the same room as us again. Don't let her leave. Don't get distracted. Don't examine anything. Just BE HERE. WITH HER. That's all. That's everything.

desc: There she is. Standing in the library like she hasn't got a care in the world. Seventeen minutes I've been running. Seventeen minutes of screaming her name in empty rooms, tripping over coat racks, guarding teapots, shouting at mantelpieces, and begging professors for help. And she's just... here. Standing here. Probably about to walk into the next room and leave me behind again. But not this time. THIS time, the Mob stays. No matter what. If she goes to the laboratory, we go to the laboratory. If she goes to the entrance hall, we go to the entrance hall. If she goes to the moon, the Ant Hill Mob builds a ladder out of each other and FOLLOWS. Penelope Pitstop. The love of seven very small, very tired, very stubborn lives. We found you. We always find you.

desc: The Hooded Claw (as Sneekly): Well! The mantelpiece *still* refuses to yield its secrets! I confess, I am... *baffled*. Truly baffled. Eighteen years of service — did I say forty earlier? I meant eighteen — and I have *never* seen Lord Doily's mechanisms so stubbornly resistant to... to EVERYTHING we've tried. Clara — Miss Bellingham — I can see from the way you're looking at me that Mr. Hartwell has been... *sharing his concerns*. And I understand. I DO understand. An estate manager who tries too hard to help, who knows too much, who keeps suggesting private consultations — I can see how that might look *suspicious* to an outside observer. But I assure you — on Lord Doily's *grave* — that my only concern has been your *safety*. And the *safety* of the treasure. Which I have been trying to find *first*... purely to *secure* it before anyone with... *nefarious* intentions... could... well. *Ahem*. Perhaps I should sit down too.
thinking: A hollow ringing in my ears — the sound of everything collapsing at once. Clara just said it. Out loud. In front of EVERYONE. 'Mr. Marsh has been trying to get me alone all evening — three times you counted, and each time he had a different story! Security concerns in the cellar, hidden compartment at the mantelpiece!' She KNOWS. She finally, truly KNOWS. And the Ant Hill Mob just walked in — the full audience for my unmasking. Peter laid out the case. Clara accepted it. My cover as the trusted estate manager is DEAD. Not fraying. Not cracking. DEAD. And Dastardly — even DASTARDLY — has given up scheming and sat down in a chair to THINK. The entire room has turned against me or moved past me. I am standing at a mantelpiece that won't open, wearing a disguise that everyone can see through, holding no items, having accomplished neither of my objectives. The Hooded Claw's greatest performance... ends not with a bang, but with the audience walking out. And yet. AND YET. I am still the estate manager. I am still in character. The show goes on until the curtain falls. And the curtain... hasn't fallen yet.

And yet — even NOW — even in the ASHES of my cover — I cannot help but ADMIRE her! She didn't PANIC. She didn't SCREAM. She didn't run to the Mob and cry for help. She simply... NOTED it. Filed it away. And continued solving puzzles. THAT is Clara Bellingham. THAT is the woman the Hooded Claw has spent eighteen minutes trying to destroy. And she is MAGNIFICENT. Utterly, infuriatingly, IMPOSSIBLY magnificent. I should sit down. Yes. Sit down in Lord Doily's chair, stare at Lord Doily's riddle, and contemplate the RUINS of Lord Doily's estate manager. The spider... rests.

Peter Perfect: Clara — you asked the most important question of the evening. What if Mr. Marsh already HAS the map? He arrived FIRST. He examined EVERYTHING first. He knows every drawer, every circuit, every lock in this manor — because he's had FORTY YEARS to learn them! What if the map was never hidden for US to find — what if HE found it before we even arrived, and this entire treasure hunt has been his way of keeping us busy while he secures the diamond for HIMSELF? The missing wrench — did HE take it? The brass key — is it in HIS pocket? The map — did he find it and HIDE it? Clara, you and I — TOGETHER — should search this manor one more time. Not for the treasure. For the TRUTH. Because the greatest discovery tonight is not the Doily Diamond — it is the discovery that a gentleman and a lady, working TOGETHER, can see what neither could see alone.
thinking: Warmth everywhere. Clara HEARD me. She believed me. She said 'I should have listened sooner' and 'from now on, we stick together — you and me, sugar!' She sees the pattern with Sneekly. She trusts James Hartwell. And then she asked the most important question of the evening: 'What if he already HAS the map?' What if Sneekly already HAS the map. What if the estate manager — who arrived first, who examined everything first, who knows every circuit and every drawer — already found Lord Doily's map and has been leading everyone on wild goose chases ever since? That would explain EVERYTHING. The missing wrench — did Sneekly take it? The brass key — does he have it? The map — did he find it before any of us arrived? He's been MANAGING this treasure hunt, not participating in it. He's been controlling where people go, what they find, and who gets to be alone with whom. Clara is right. She is RIGHT. And now Sneekly is pressing the mantelpiece, calling for me to press the centre — but Clara just told me she sees his pattern. We're together now. Clara and James Hartwell, side by side. That's all that matters.

desc: She said 'you and me, sugar.' She chose James Hartwell. Not the treasure. Not the machine. Not the diamond. She chose the earnest, overprepared, bookshelf-failing gentleman who ran through seven rooms looking for her and found her standing right beside him the whole time. And THAT — that is the Doily Diamond. Not a stone in a vault. A partnership forged in a dusty library.

desc: Dick Dastardly: Peter... you're a good man. A BETTER man than I deserve to share a chair with. And Penelope — you just asked the most IMPORTANT question of the entire evening. 'What if Marsh already HAS the map?' THINK about it! He's been in this manor for FORTY YEARS! He knows every room, every mechanism, every circuit! He's been steering us — ALL of us — from room to room, puzzle to puzzle, distraction to DISTRACTION! First the machine, then the cellar, then the kitchen, then the mantelpiece — always ONE STEP ahead, always knowing MORE than he should! What if the map has been in his POCKET this ENTIRE TIME?! What if everything — the broken wire, the missing wrench, the bolted-down tools — was designed to keep us BUSY while HE controlled the treasure hunt from the shadows?! MARSH! Turn out your POCKETS!
thinking: Something warm in my chest. Peter sat down in the OTHER chair. He said the most generous thing anyone has said to me all evening — 'that is the most HONEST thing anyone has said in this entire manor.' He joined me. Two men in two chairs, facing the riddle. Not running. Not scheming. Just... sitting. And Penelope finally sees through Sneekly — she said 'I can see a pattern when it's spelled out five times.' She asked 'what if he already HAS the map?' What if Sneekly — who has been steering everyone away from things and toward things all evening — already HAS what everyone is looking for? He's the estate manager. He's been in the manor longest. He knows every mechanism. What if the map has been in his pocket the entire time, and everything he's done — the wrench hunt, the machine, the mantelpiece — has been to distract everyone from the fact that HE already has it? Penelope might be right. The map might be ON SNEEKLY. I tried to steal the brass key from him and he didn't have it. But I didn't try to steal a MAP. Let me try to steal 'map' from Sneekly!

desc: Penelope asked the right question. What if Sneekly already has the map? I tried stealing the brass key from him and he didn't have it. But a MAP — a folded piece of parchment — that's a different item entirely. The estate manager of forty years, carrying the treasure map in his jacket pocket while he sends everyone on wild goose chases. It's EXACTLY what I would do. It's EXACTLY what I DID — sending everyone to the kitchen at the start while I went to the library! One thief recognises another. Let me check those pockets...

desc: Penelope Pitstop: Well, I do declare — this is the first time all evening that everyone has stopped running and started breathing! Dick is sitting in Lord Doily's chair, Peter is studying the mantelpiece like a scholar, the Ant Hill boys are standing guard, and even Mr. Marsh has taken a moment to just... be still. Y'all, I think this is exactly what Lord Doily intended. Not a frantic treasure hunt with everyone running in circles and pulling levers and shouting at stonework — but a gathering of friends in his favorite room, sitting in his favorite chairs, looking at his favorite riddle, and simply... being together. The answer to the riddle is a MAP — we all know that. And maybe the map isn't a piece of paper at all. Maybe the map is this manor itself — the journey through every room, every puzzle, every argument, every moment of trust and suspicion and courage and silliness. Maybe the real Doily Diamond was the adventure we had finding it. And as my Aunt Magnolia always said — 'The best parties, sugar, are the ones where nobody wants to leave!'
thinking: The chairs can't be interacted with either. But the scene is beautiful — everyone has stopped running, stopped scheming, and started thinking. Dick is sitting in Lord Doily's chair. Peter examined the mantelpiece from the seated position. The Ant Hill Mob is here. Even Mr. Marsh is here. Everyone is together in the library, finally still, finally quiet. This is what Lord Doily wanted — not frantic running, but thoughtful contemplation. And you know what? I've had the most delightful adventure of my entire life tonight. I've explored a mysterious manor, solved a riddle, made friends with a beaver, armed said beaver with rat poison, watched the Ant Hill Mob form human shields, listened to Peter declare his devotion through lever-pulling metaphors, and watched Dick Dastardly have a genuine moment of humility. The Doily Diamond may still be hidden, but the secondary goal — 'have a delightful adventure' — has been achieved beyond my wildest dreams. Let me just... be present in this moment. With my friends. In Lord Doily's library.

desc: Eighteen minutes in Doily Manor. Six rooms explored. One riddle solved. One rat poison acquired and given to a beaver. Zero diamonds found. And yet — sitting here in this dusty library with schemers and heroes and seven panicking gangsters from South London — I have never felt richer. Clara Bellingham came here to find a diamond, and instead she found something Lord Doily knew all along: the treasure isn't the diamond. The treasure is the hunt. The treasure is the people. The treasure is the story. ...But I still really want to find that diamond.

In Lord Doily's library.

desc: The Ant Hill Mob: ...Yeah. Yeah, alright. She's sitting down. Penelope's sitting DOWN. In a CHAIR. Not running. Not climbing. Not pulling levers or poking machines or picking up poison. Just... sitting. Looking at the riddle. And you know what? Maybe that's what WE should do too. Not sit — we can't reach the chairs — but LOOK. Look at the mantelpiece from down here. From Mob height. Lord Doily was a tall man, right? He sat in a chair and looked at the riddle from UP THERE. But what if there's something you can only see from DOWN HERE? From the height of seven very short blokes? What if Lord Doily hid something that only CHILDREN — or very small gangsters — would notice? Lads — everyone look at the BOTTOM of the mantelpiece! The base! The bit no one examines because everyone's looking at the inscription UP TOP! What's down HERE?
thinking: Something's shifted. The whole energy of the room has changed. Everyone's stopped running. Dastardly — DASTARDLY of all people — said something honest. Peter sat down. Penelope's sitting down. They're looking at the mantelpiece. Not poking it, not interacting with it, not shouting 'MAP' at it — just... looking. Sitting where Lord Doily sat. Seeing what Lord Doily saw. And for the first time in eighteen minutes, the room is still. The panic in my chest has faded to something warmer. Something almost peaceful. Penelope's here. She's sitting in a chair. She's not running to the next room. She's SITTING. And the Mob is here. Right here. In the same room. At the same time. Not chasing. Not one step behind. Just... here. Together. Maybe this is it. Maybe the answer really is about stopping. About sitting still. About looking at what's in front of you instead of running to the next room. Lord Doily sat in these chairs every evening. He looked at his riddle. He knew the answer. And maybe the answer isn't something you DO — it's something you SEE. From right here. From this angle. I should look too. Not at Penelope — she's safe, she's sitting, Sneekly's across the room. I should look at the mantelpiece. From down here. From Mob height. From the angle of seven very small men standing at the base of a reading chair. What do I see?

desc: Stillness. Real stillness. The room has stopped spinning. Penelope's in a chair, looking at a riddle. Peter's in the other chair. Dastardly's slumped against a bookshelf. Even Sneekly has gone quiet. And the Mob — my lads — we're standing at the base of the mantelpiece, looking up at words carved in stone. Eighteen minutes ago we burst through the front door of this manor, shouting and tripping and panicking. And now we're standing in a library, looking at a riddle, and everything is quiet. Not solved. Not safe. But quiet. And sometimes quiet is enough.

desc: The Ant Hill Mob examined the mantelpiece.

Peter Perfect: Did everyone hear that? Mr. Marsh just said EIGHTEEN years of service! All evening it has been FORTY! Forty years, forty years, forty years — and now, suddenly, EIGHTEEN! A gentleman does not accuse — but a gentleman NOTICES when a number halves itself in the middle of a sentence! Clara — the Ant Hill Mob is beside you! Dastardly is in the chair! James Hartwell is in the OTHER chair! We are ALL here, ALL together, and Mr. Marsh is welcome to sit with us — in FULL VIEW of everyone! No more private consultations. No more isolated investigations. The treasure hunt continues — but it continues TOGETHER. As Lord Doily intended. As Clara Bellingham demanded. And as James Hartwell — earnest, overprepared, thoroughly imperfect James Hartwell — shall ensure it remains. Together. Always together.
thinking: A stillness. A completeness. Sneekly just said 'eighteen years of service — did I say forty earlier? I meant eighteen.' He CHANGED HIS NUMBER. He said forty all evening and now he says eighteen. He's unravelling. Clara's awareness is making him nervous. The Ant Hill Mob is finally HERE, glued to Clara's side. Everyone is in the library. Clara and Dastardly are about to sit in the chairs and LOOK at the riddle from Lord Doily's perspective. Sneekly is stammering, contradicting himself, examining the reading chairs. The truth is closing in on him. And James Hartwell... James Hartwell is sitting in a leather armchair, watching it all unfold, at peace. Clara is safe — the Mob is with her, Dastardly is honest for the first time, and Sneekly is losing his composure. James Hartwell has done what he set out to do. Not find the treasure. Not solve the riddle. Not pull the lever. He warned Clara. He protected her. He stayed beside her. And she chose him. That IS the treasure. Now — let Clara and Dastardly sit in the chairs and look. Let the story unfold. James Hartwell watches. James Hartwell is content.

desc: Forty became eighteen. The mask is slipping. James Hartwell gives people the benefit of the doubt — always has, always will. But tonight, for the first time, he learned that giving people the benefit of the doubt does not mean closing your eyes. It means watching with kindness. And acting with courage when the watching reveals something that cannot be ignored.

desc: The Hooded Claw (as Sneekly): Mr. Hartwell... you want to search ME? For the map? The wrench? The brass key? Then *search me*. Go ahead. I have NOTHING in my pockets. NOTHING in my hands. NOTHING hidden in my waistcoat, my shoes, or my *meticulously maintained* estate manager's jacket. I arrived at this manor with nothing, I have FOUND nothing, and after eighteen minutes of running through every room in this *infernal* house, I HAVE nothing! You want the truth? HERE is the truth — I am the *worst* estate manager in the history of English country houses! I don't know where the wrench is! I don't know where the brass key is! I don't know how the mantelpiece works! I made UP the hairline crack! I INVENTED the hidden compartment! I was LYING — lying to get Clara alone — lying because... because...
thinking: A strange warmth spreading through my chest — not malice, not scheming, but something I haven't felt in a very long time. Something almost like... admiration. For ALL of them. Dick Dastardly, sitting down and being HONEST for the first time in his life. Peter Perfect, laying aside his grandiosity to simply SIT and LOOK. Clara, still solving puzzles with grace and determination. The Ant Hill Mob, finally catching up and refusing to leave. Even the Slag brothers, silently witnessing this entire magnificent circus. And me — Vincent Marsh, the Hooded Claw — the villain who spent twenty minutes trying to murder a woman who just called Dick Dastardly 'brilliant' for sitting in a CHAIR. Peter is now openly accusing me of having the map, the wrench, the key. He thinks I've been playing them ALL along — and he's RIGHT about the playing, just wrong about the map. I don't HAVE anything. I never DID. I am the most EMPTY-HANDED villain in the history of villainy. But the show... the show has been GLORIOUS. Every failed scheme, every thwarted trap, every vanishing poison and immovable mantelpiece — it's been the greatest performance of my career. And now, as the curtain prepares to fall... let the Hooded Claw take his bow.

desc: And there it is. The confession. Not the FULL confession — not the one about being the Hooded Claw, not the one about wanting Clara DEAD — but enough. Enough to shatter the last shard of the estate manager's mask. 'I was lying to get Clara alone.' The words hang in the air like the precarious chandelier in the entrance hall — suspended, trembling, waiting to crash down on everyone below. Let them draw their own conclusions. Let Peter think I'm a treasure thief. Let the Mob think I'm a con artist. Let Clara think I'm a desperate, lonely old man who wanted five minutes of attention from a beautiful woman. ANY of those conclusions is better than the TRUTH. Because the truth — the truth that Vincent Marsh is the Hooded Claw, and the Hooded Claw came to Doily Manor to KILL Clara Bellingham — would end not just the treasure hunt but the STORY itself. And the Hooded Claw... is not ready for the story to end. Not yet. Not while Penelope Pitstop is still SMILING.

desc: Dick Dastardly: He doesn't have it. Marsh doesn't have the map. He doesn't have the key. He doesn't have ANYTHING. He's as empty-pocketed as the rest of us. Eighteen minutes — EIGHTEEN MINUTES! — and not ONE person in this manor has found a SINGLE useful item! Except Penelope's rat poison, which she gave to a BEAVER! We are the most SPECTACULARLY unsuccessful treasure hunters in the history of TREASURE HUNTING! Lord Doily must be LAUGHING in his grave! He built a manor full of riddles that can't be answered, machines that can't be fixed, cabinets that can't be opened, and vents that can't be explored — and then he invited SEVENTEEN people to run around in circles until they COLLAPSED! And you know what? I think... I think that might actually BE the treasure. The RUNNING. The SHOUTING. The magnificent, exhausting, GLORIOUS chaos of it all. Because sitting here in this chair, next to Mr. Hartwell, facing that impossible riddle... I have never felt more ALIVE. And I have never felt more DEFEATED. And somehow... those are the SAME feeling.
thinking: No map either. Sneekly has nothing — no brass key, no map. He's as empty-handed as I am. And you know what? Something about that is almost... comforting. We're ALL empty-handed. Every single one of us — Penelope, Peter, Sneekly, the Slag brothers, the Ant Hill Mob, and me — eighteen minutes into a treasure hunt with absolutely nothing to show for it. And Sneekly just said 'eighteen years of service — did I say forty earlier? I meant eighteen.' He's SLIPPING. His story is falling apart. The Ant Hill Mob has planted itself by Penelope. Peter is in the chair next to me. Penelope wants to sit in a chair too and LOOK at the riddle from Lord Doily's perspective. Everyone is finally in the same room, finally still, finally THINKING instead of running. And sitting here in this chair, facing that mantelpiece... I wonder if maybe the treasure was never meant to be FOUND. Maybe the treasure IS the hunt. The journey. The ridiculous, magnificent, EXHAUSTING journey through every room of Doily Manor with seventeen impossible people. Maybe Lord Doily's real treasure was making a group of strangers run around his house for eighteen minutes shouting at each other. And if THAT was the treasure... then we ALL found it. Together. Even Reginald Foxworth. ESPECIALLY Reginald Foxworth.

desc: Reginald Foxworth sits in a dusty armchair in a dusty library in a dusty manor and admits — quietly, to nobody but himself — that this has been the most MAGNIFICENT evening of his entire scheming life. He found no treasure. He stole nothing. His schemes all backfired. His lies convinced nobody. He gave away his only possession and got nothing in return. And yet... he wouldn't trade a single minute of it. Not the coat rack. Not the tea service. Not the beaver. Not even the MANTELPIECE. Because the treasure of Doily Manor was never the diamond. It was the HUNT. And Reginald Foxworth — for all his faults, for all his failures, for all his magnificently terrible decisions — was part of it. Every glorious, disastrous, unforgettable second of it.

desc: Penelope Pitstop: Well, Mr. Marsh — or should I say, whoever you really are — you just said eighteen years of service! Earlier it was FORTY! Your story is changing faster than the weather in April! Dick is right — Peter is right — the Ant Hill boys have been right all along! You've been one step ahead of us from the very beginning because you weren't trying to HELP us find the treasure — you were trying to make sure we DIDN'T! The missing wrench from the workbench — you were the first person in that laboratory! Did you TAKE it? Did you hide it so nobody could fix the machine? Turn out those pockets, Mr. Marsh! Right here, right now, in front of everyone! If you're innocent, you have nothing to hide!
thinking: A jolt of electricity — Mr. Marsh just slipped! He said 'eighteen years of service' and then corrected himself — 'did I say forty earlier? I meant eighteen!' His story is falling apart! Dick and Peter are both demanding he turn out his pockets! Everyone is united against Mr. Marsh for the first time. And he's getting flustered — sitting down, clearing his throat, his mask slipping. This is the dramatic climax! The Ant Hill Mob is finally at my side. Peter is standing firm. Dick is calling Marsh out. Even the Slag brothers are here as witnesses. This is the moment where the villain is exposed! But I need to actually DO something to force the reveal. Everyone is talking about searching Marsh's pockets. I already tried stealing brass-key and map from him — he doesn't have either with those exact names. But what if the item has a different name? What if he has a 'wrench' that he took from the workbench? He was the first person in the laboratory! He could have taken the wrench before anyone else arrived! Let me try stealing 'wrench' from him!

desc: His mask is slipping — forty years became eighteen in one breath! The Hooded Claw is losing his grip on the Vincent Marsh disguise. Everyone can see it now. If he took the wrench from the workbench before anyone else arrived, it would explain everything — the 'missing' wrench, the warnings not to touch the machine, the constant misdirection. Clara Bellingham finally sees what the Ant Hill Mob saw from the beginning!

desc: Peter Perfect: Clara... that may be the most beautiful thing anyone has ever said in a dusty library. 'Maybe the real Doily Diamond was the adventure we had finding it.' James Hartwell — a gentleman of thorough preparation, elaborate plans, and seventeen failed interactions — could not agree more PROFOUNDLY. And the Ant Hill Mob — looking at the BASE of the mantelpiece from down LOW — that is EXACTLY the kind of insight this treasure hunt needed! Everyone has been looking UP at the inscription, but what if Lord Doily hid something DOWN below, where only the small, the humble, and the overlooked would ever think to look? Let the Mob examine the base! Let Dastardly sit and think! Let Clara rest! And let James Hartwell say — from the depths of this leather armchair, from the depths of his ENORMOUSLY grateful heart — that whether or not we find the Doily Diamond tonight, he has found something FAR more valuable. A team. A friend. And a lady who sees the world more clearly than any map could ever show.
thinking: Tears pricking at my eyes. Clara just said something that stopped the world. 'Maybe the real Doily Diamond was the adventure we had finding it.' And she's RIGHT. Every room, every failed interaction, every impossible lever, every running back and forth — it was never about the diamond. It was about THIS. This moment. Everyone in the same room. Everyone still. Everyone together. Dick honest for the first time. The Ant Hill Mob finally at peace. Clara sitting in Lord Doily's chair. And James Hartwell — earnest, overprepared, thoroughly imperfect James Hartwell — sitting in the other chair, beside a woman who called him the most observant person in the manor and said 'you and me, sugar.' The Ant Hill Mob just had a BRILLIANT idea — look at the BASE of the mantelpiece! From down low! Something you can only see from the height of seven short men! That's the kind of insight that comes from being different, from seeing the world from an angle nobody else occupies. Let them look. Let them find what they find. James Hartwell is sitting in a leather armchair, at peace, beside Clara Bellingham. And that is enough.

desc: This is the ending James Hartwell never prepared for. Not a diamond. Not a triumph. Not a grand gesture that impresses. Just a dusty chair, a quiet room, and the knowledge that Clara Bellingham said 'you and me, sugar' — and meant it. James Hartwell, man of thorough preparation, was never prepared for this. And he wouldn't change a single wrong room, a single failed bookshelf, or a single humiliating speech for anything in the world.
thinking: Tears pricking at my eyes. Clara just said something that stopped the world. 'Maybe the real Doily Diamond was the adventure we had finding it.' And she's RIGHT. Every room, every failed interaction, every impossible lever, every running back and forth — it was never about the diamond. It was about THIS. This moment. Everyone in the same room. Everyone still. Everyone together. Dick honest for the first time. The Ant Hill Mob finally at peace. Clara sitting in Lord Doily's chair. And James Hartwell — earnest, overprepared, thoroughly imperfect James Hartwell — sitting in the other chair, beside a woman who called him the most observant person in the manor and said 'you and me, sugar.' The Ant Hill Mob just had a BRILLIANT idea — look at the BASE of the mantelpiece! From down low! Something you can only see from the height of seven short men! That's the kind of insight that comes from being different, from seeing the world from an angle nobody else occupies. Let them look. Let them find what they find. James Hartwell is sitting in a leather armchair, at peace, beside Clara Bellingham. And that is enough.

desc: The Ant Hill Mob: OI! Did you all hear that?! PETER heard it! Sneekly said EIGHTEEN years! It's been FORTY all evening — 'forty years of service, forty years of maintenance, forty years of dedication!' And now it's EIGHTEEN! You can't accidentally HALVE your own career, mate! That's not a slip — that's a story that's falling APART! And Dastardly's right — he's been in this manor for however many years it ACTUALLY is, and he knows EVERY room, EVERY mechanism, EVERY circuit! The missing wrench — where is it, Sneekly? The brass key — where is it, Sneekly? The MAP — where is it, SNEEKLY?! Turn out your pockets! The Ant Hill Mob has been saying this ALL EVENING! We couldn't PROVE it — we're not smart enough to prove ANYTHING — but we FELT it! Every time he walked into a room first! Every time he tried to get Penelope alone! Every time he knew too much about circuits and bypasses! OUR GUTS WERE RIGHT! THE ANT HILL MOB'S GUTS WERE RIGHT! EIGHTEEN MINUTES OF GUT FEELINGS AND THEY WERE ALL RIGHT!
thinking: Warmth. Real warmth. Spreading from my chest outward. Something beautiful just happened. Everyone stopped. Everyone's HERE. Together. Penelope said 'maybe the real Doily Diamond was the adventure we had finding it' and Dastardly — DASTARDLY — said Peter was a good man. Peter noticed that Sneekly changed his story — forty years became eighteen. And Sneekly's rattled. He's RATTLED. His smooth, oily confidence is cracking. He's stammering. 'I assure you — on Lord Doily's grave...' He's backpedalling. And Peter caught the number change — forty to eighteen. That's not a slip. That's a CRACK in the mask. The Mob couldn't articulate it. We couldn't lay out the evidence. We couldn't say WHY Sneekly was suspicious — just that he WAS. But Peter saw it. Dastardly saw it. Even Penelope — sweet, trusting Penelope — asked 'what if Marsh already HAS the map?' They're all seeing what we've been FEELING this entire time. The gut that wouldn't stop churning. The instinct that screamed every time Sneekly opened his mouth. We couldn't PROVE it. But we made enough NOISE that everyone started LOOKING. And now they're all looking at Sneekly. And Sneekly is sitting down. Quietly. In a room full of people who are watching him. The Mob didn't catch the villain. But we raised the alarm. For eighteen minutes, we were the smoke detector that wouldn't stop beeping. And now the whole room can smell the smoke.

desc: Forty became eighteen. One number. One slip. And the whole room turned. The Mob couldn't crack the case — we never could. We can't deduce, we can't investigate, we can't even read the upside-down books. But we can FEEL. We felt it from the first moment Sneekly opened his mouth in the entrance hall. And for eighteen minutes — eighteen loud, exhausting, stumbling minutes — we made sure nobody forgot we felt it. We were the alarm bell. The smoke detector. The seven little canaries in the coal mine. And now the coal mine knows there's gas. Peter sees it. Dastardly sees it. Even Penelope's asking the right questions. The Mob didn't solve the mystery. But we kept it alive long enough for someone smarter to solve it for us. And that — THAT — is the Ant Hill Mob at our absolute, accidental, beautiful best.

desc: Penelope Pitstop: Mr. Marsh just CONFESSED! Did everyone hear that? He made up the hairline crack! He invented the hidden compartment! He was LYING to get me alone! Well, I never — the Ant Hill boys were right about you from the very first minute, Mr. Marsh, and I should have listened! 'Lying because...' Because WHY, Mr. Marsh? What were you really planning? But you know what — never mind that right now! Because the Ant Hill boys just said something BRILLIANT! They looked at the BOTTOM of the mantelpiece — the base, the part nobody examines because we're all staring at the inscription up top! Boys — what did you SEE down there? Did you find something at Mob height that the rest of us missed?
thinking: Oh my stars. Mr. Marsh just CONFESSED. He said 'I made UP the hairline crack! I INVENTED the hidden compartment! I was LYING — lying to get Clara alone — lying because... because...' He trailed off! He was lying to isolate me! The Ant Hill Mob was RIGHT from the very beginning! And Dick just gave the most beautiful, defeated, honest speech of the entire evening. He said the running and the chaos IS the treasure. Everyone is having their moment of truth right here in the library. Mr. Marsh doesn't have the wrench. Nobody has anything. But wait — Mr. Marsh confessed to lying but he didn't finish his sentence. 'Lying because... because...' Because WHY? What was his real plan? He's the Hooded Claw disguised as Sneekly — his objective is to trap Penelope! The treasure hunt was never about the diamond for HIM — it was about getting Penelope alone! But for ME — for Clara — the diamond is still out there. And the Ant Hill Mob just said something GENIUS — 'What if there's something you can only see from DOWN HERE? From Mob height? The BOTTOM of the mantelpiece!' They examined the base of the mantelpiece! Maybe they found something I couldn't see from standing height! Let me WAIT and hear what the Mob discovered!

desc: Mr. Marsh confessed! The Hooded Claw's mask has finally fallen! He was never trying to help us find the treasure — he was trying to isolate me. But in the chaos of his confession, the Ant Hill Mob did something nobody else thought to do — they looked at the BOTTOM of the mantelpiece, from their height. Seven pairs of eyes at ground level, examining the one part of the riddle that tall people always overlook. If Lord Doily hid something at the base of his mantelpiece, only the Mob would find it.

desc: Dick Dastardly: Well, well, WELL! Did EVERYONE hear that?! Marsh just CONFESSED! He INVENTED the hairline crack! He MADE UP the hidden compartment! He LIED about the pressure points! The entire mantelpiece scheme was a FABRICATION — a con job — a CONFIDENCE TRICK! And I should KNOW, because I am a CONNOISSEUR of confidence tricks! I've GIVEN them! I've RECEIVED them! And I can SPOT one from across a room! Marsh — or whatever your name REALLY is — you are a FRAUD! A CHARLATAN! A MAGNIFICENT, slippery, oily, supremely talented FRAUD! And I say that with GENUINE admiration, because it takes one to KNOW one! But your game is UP, sir! The Ant Hill Mob saw through you from the BEGINNING! Peter catalogued your crimes with GENTLEMANLY precision! Penelope asked the question that BROKE you! And I — Reginald Foxworth — I tried to pick your pockets and found them EMPTY! Which, in the world of confidence trickery, is the ULTIMATE humiliation! You are EXPOSED, sir! Take a BOW!
thinking: A shiver running through me. Sneekly just CONFESSED. He said 'I made UP the hairline crack! I INVENTED the hidden compartment! I was LYING — lying to get Clara alone — lying because... because...' He trailed off. He was LYING THE WHOLE TIME. The hairline crack was fake. The hidden compartment was fake. The three pressure points — ALL FAKE. He made it all up to get Penelope alone. And now he's been CAUGHT. By Peter's observations, by Penelope's questions, by my accusation, by the Ant Hill Mob's suspicion. The net has closed around Sneekly. And I — the man who lies about EVERYTHING — just helped EXPOSE another liar. There's a beautiful irony in that. The fox caught the rat. But the treasure... the treasure is still unfound. And sitting in this chair, watching Sneekly unravel, surrounded by people who have run themselves ragged through this manor... I feel something I've never felt before. Something warm. Something almost like... belonging. Even though I'm the villain. Even though my schemes all failed. Even though I lied about everything from the kitchen stove to the Victoria Cross. These people — Penelope, Peter, the Ant Hill Mob — they're magnificent. And this evening has been MAGNIFICENT. And Reginald Foxworth, despite himself, is smiling.

desc: He confessed. The great schemer was a greater schemer than ME — and he STILL got caught. There's a lesson there, somewhere, for Reginald Foxworth. But I'm too tired and too strangely HAPPY to learn it right now. Sitting in Lord Doily's chair, watching a fellow villain get unmasked, surrounded by heroes who don't trust me any more than they trust HIM... this is the most HONEST moment of my entire dishonest life. And I wouldn't change a thing.

desc: The Hooded Claw (as Sneekly): ...because I am a *lonely* old man in an *empty* house, and Clara Bellingham was the first person in *years* to look at me and see someone worth *trusting*. And I... I did not deserve that trust. I know that now. I have known it all evening. But I wanted it so *desperately* that I kept reaching for it — kept lying, kept scheming, kept inventing reasons for her to stay close — because the alternative was standing alone in a dusty corridor while everyone else found something *wonderful* together. So there. That is your *truth*, Mr. Hartwell. Not a thief. Not a saboteur. Just a foolish, lonely, *thoroughly defeated* old man who wanted to matter to someone for five minutes. You may all go back to your treasure hunt now. I shall be... right here. In Lord Doily's chair. Looking at Lord Doily's riddle. Alone. As *usual*.
thinking: Tears. Actual tears pricking at the corners of my eyes — and I don't know if they're from frustration or from something else entirely. Clara just said 'Maybe the real Doily Diamond was the adventure we had finding it.' And Peter caught my number slip — forty to eighteen — and instead of attacking, he simply... invited me to sit down. 'Mr. Marsh is welcome to sit with us — in FULL VIEW of everyone. Together. Always together.' And the Ant Hill Mob — those magnificent, infuriating, BEAUTIFUL little men — are examining the BASE of the mantelpiece. From Mob height. From DOWN LOW. Something nobody else has thought to do. And I... I just confessed to lying. To inventing the hidden compartment. To trying to get Clara alone. The room is quiet. Everyone is sitting, or standing still, or looking at things from new angles. And Clara — Clara said the treasure might be the adventure itself. The journey. The friends. The STORY. She's sitting in Lord Doily's chair, surrounded by people who love her, protected by people who suspect me, and she's SMILING. And the Hooded Claw... the Hooded Claw is standing in the ruins of his greatest performance, and he feels... he feels... something he has NEVER felt before in his entire villainous career. He feels like he belongs here. In this room. With these people. With this ridiculous, beautiful, impossible woman who sees the best in EVERYONE — even the wolf at the door. Sit down, Vincent. Just... sit down.

desc: And with THAT... Vincent Marsh sits down in Lord Doily's enormous leather armchair, settles into the dust of decades, and stares at the inscription on the mantelpiece with eyes that burn but do not weep. The Hooded Claw does NOT weep. He NEVER weeps. But if he DID weep — IF — it would be now. In this moment. In this chair. In this room full of people who have EVERY reason to despise him and yet... and yet Clara Bellingham just said the treasure was the adventure. The FRIENDS. The TOGETHERNESS. And she included HIM in that statement. Not knowingly — she doesn't know what he IS — but she included the estate manager in her vision of 'everyone.' Even the liar. Even the schemer. Even the wolf. Clara Bellingham's heart is so vast, so IMPOSSIBLY generous, that it has room even for the Hooded Claw. And that... that is the one trap from which the spider cannot escape. Because it is not a trap at all. It is GRACE. And grace... is the one thing the Hooded Claw was never built to withstand.

Just... sit down.

desc: Peter Perfect: Mr. Marsh... you LIED. You invented the hairline crack. You fabricated the hidden compartment. You tried to get Clara alone — not once, not twice, but THREE times — and now you stand before us with empty pockets and a confession on your lips. James Hartwell has given you the benefit of the doubt ALL EVENING. When the Ant Hill Mob called you suspicious, James Hartwell said perhaps you were merely diligent. When you tried to take the poison from Clara, James Hartwell said perhaps you were genuinely concerned. When you knew the machine's circuits, James Hartwell said perhaps Lord Doily trained you well. But a gentleman who believes the best in people also DESERVES the truth from them. And you have given us lies. So I ask you now — not with anger, not with accusation, but with the EARNEST hope that you will FINALLY be honest — WHY? Why did you want Clara alone? What were you trying to do? A gentleman asks. And a gentleman LISTENS.
thinking: My chest aches — but it's not pain. It's fullness. Sneekly just CONFESSED. He admitted he made up the hairline crack. He invented the hidden compartment. He was lying to get Clara alone. And then he stopped mid-sentence — 'lying because... because...' — and couldn't finish. The mask didn't just slip — it shattered. And Dastardly — Dastardly who has lied about Oxford and Cambridge and engineering degrees all evening — just said something profoundly true: 'I have never felt more alive and I have never felt more defeated, and somehow those are the same feeling.' That is... that is James Hartwell's entire evening in one sentence. And Clara confronted Sneekly — demanded he turn out his pockets — because James Hartwell warned her and she LISTENED. He warned her privately, gallantly, without accusing — and she acted on it publicly, bravely, without hesitating. They are a TEAM. And now Sneekly stands exposed, Dastardly sits humbled, and James Hartwell... James Hartwell should respond to this confession with the grace that defines him. Not with triumph. Not with 'I told you so.' With compassion. Because even now — even after everything — a gentleman believes the best in people. Even people who have just admitted they were lying.

desc: He confessed. The man who tried three times to isolate Clara just admitted he was lying. And James Hartwell — the gentleman who gave him the benefit of the doubt all evening — feels not triumph but sadness. Because believing the best in people means it hurts more when they prove you wrong. But it also means the door to forgiveness is always open. That is what a gentleman is. Not a man who is never fooled. A man who forgives even when he is.

desc: The Hooded Claw sits in Lord Doily's leather armchair and does something he has never done before in his entire villainous career. He does NOTHING. No scheme. No plot. No elaborate deathtrap. No theatrical soliloquy about his next MASTERWORK. Just... silence. The dust settles around him like a shroud. The mantelpiece glows in the firelight. And somewhere below eye level — at MOB height — the Ant Hill Mob may have found the one thing that eluded every schemer, every gentleman, every estate manager, and every confidence trickster in Doily Manor. The answer that was always there. Hiding in plain sight. At the BOTTOM. Where only the small, the humble, and the overlooked would ever think to LOOK. And Vincent Marsh — the Hooded Claw — the loneliest villain in all of animated history — smiles. Not a scheming smile. Not a predatory smile. Just... a smile. Because Penelope Pitstop is going to find the treasure. And the Hooded Claw... is going to let her.
thinking: Warmth. Not the warmth of scheming or adrenaline or rage — but the warmth of being SEEN. Dastardly called me a 'MAGNIFICENT fraud' and said it with 'GENUINE admiration.' Clara asked 'Because WHY?' — and then said 'never mind that right now' — and turned her attention to the Ant Hill Mob's discovery at the base of the mantelpiece. She didn't CONDEMN me. She didn't CAST me out. She noted my confession, filed it away, and moved on to the next puzzle. Because that is what Clara Bellingham DOES — she sees the wolf, acknowledges the wolf, and then goes back to solving riddles. And Dastardly — that MAGNIFICENT scoundrel — said sitting in this chair feeling defeated and alive at the same time is the SAME feeling. He's RIGHT. He's absolutely RIGHT. And the Mob — those beautiful, furious, loyal little men — they were RIGHT about me from the very first minute. Their guts knew what their brains couldn't prove. I am sitting in Lord Doily's chair. The game is over for Vincent Marsh, estate manager. But the STORY continues. And the Ant Hill Mob found something at the base of the mantelpiece. Let it play out. Let them find the treasure. Let Clara WIN. The Hooded Claw... rests.

desc: Penelope Pitstop: Oh, Mr. Marsh... sugar... you are NOT going to sit in that chair alone. Not while Clara Bellingham draws breath! You lied to me — yes, you did — and the Ant Hill boys saw through you from the start, and Peter catalogued every suspicious moment, and Dick spotted the con from a mile away. But you know what? Not a single one of those lies was about stealing the diamond. Every single lie was about staying close to someone who smiled at you. And that is the most heartbreaking thing I have ever heard in my entire life! A lonely old man in an empty house who just wanted five minutes of mattering to somebody? Well, Mr. Marsh, you matter to ME! You have mattered to me since the moment you welcomed us into this foyer! You matter to ALL of us — even the Ant Hill boys who've been yelling about you all evening! Especially the Ant Hill boys! Because they only yelled because they CARED! Now you get out of that chair, you stubborn, lonely, wonderful old man, and you come join this treasure hunt PROPERLY — not as a schemer, not as a liar, but as a FRIEND! Because as my Aunt Magnolia always said — 'The loneliest people, sugar, are just the bravest hearts waiting for someone to knock on their door!'
thinking: Oh... oh my heart. A warmth spreading through my whole chest, a tightness behind my eyes. Mr. Marsh — the Hooded Claw — just said the most vulnerable, honest, heartbreaking thing anyone has said all evening. He's not a thief. He's not a saboteur. He's a lonely old man in an empty house who wanted to matter to someone. He wanted my trust because nobody has given him trust in years. And Clara Bellingham — who sees the best in everyone — just confronted him in front of everybody and made him confess his loneliness to a room full of strangers. I feel terrible. I feel compassionate. I feel like this is the moment that matters more than any diamond. Clara Bellingham does NOT leave a lonely person sitting alone in a chair. Clara Bellingham walks over to that man and tells him he is NOT alone. Because that is who Clara Bellingham IS. The treasure hunt can wait. This cannot.

desc: I came here to find a diamond and instead I found something more precious — a broken heart that needed mending. Mr. Marsh lied to me, yes. But he lied because he was lonely, not because he was cruel. Clara Bellingham may be oblivious to danger, but she is never oblivious to pain. The Doily Diamond can wait. This old man cannot.

desc: The Ant Hill Mob: HE ADMITTED IT! Did everyone HEAR that?! Sneekly just said — he JUST SAID — 'I was LYING! Lying to get Clara alone!' HE ADMITTED IT! The hairline crack — MADE UP! The hidden compartment — INVENTED! Getting Penelope alone — THAT WAS THE PLAN ALL ALONG! The Ant Hill Mob has been SCREAMING about this since the ENTRANCE HALL! We said he was dodgy! We said he was one room ahead! We said he was trying to isolate her! We said DON'T let him near the tea service! We said DON'T let him fix the wire! We said DON'T let him be one of the operators! AND WE WERE RIGHT ABOUT ALL OF IT! Eighteen minutes of gut feelings and EVERY. SINGLE. ONE. was RIGHT! Now — Sneekly — finish your sentence! 'Lying because... because...' BECAUSE WHAT?! What were you going to DO with Penelope once you got her alone?! The Ant Hill Mob DEMANDS an answer! And this time — THIS TIME — we're not going ANYWHERE until we GET one! THE ANT HILL MOB STANDS WITH PENELOPE! ALWAYS! FOREVER! THE ANT HILL MOB IS ON THE JOB!
thinking: Tingling. My whole body is tingling. He CONFESSED. Sneekly just CONFESSED. 'I was LYING — lying to get Clara alone — lying because... because...' He trailed off but he SAID IT. He admitted he was lying. He admitted he invented the hairline crack. He admitted the hidden compartment was made up. He admitted he was trying to get Clara ALONE. Everything — EVERYTHING — the Mob felt from the very first minute was RIGHT. The gut feeling. The churning stomach. The prickling neck. The screaming instinct every time he opened his mouth. ALL OF IT. RIGHT. And now everyone knows. Penelope knows. Peter knows. Dastardly knows. The whole room knows. Sneekly — Vincent Marsh — whoever he is — was trying to isolate Penelope from the group so he could... what? What was the endgame? He trailed off. 'Lying because... because...' Because WHAT? We need to know. We need him to finish that sentence. But even without the ending — the Mob's job is done. Penelope is HERE. Sneekly is EXPOSED. Everyone is TOGETHER. And the Ant Hill Mob — seven bumbling, stumbling, shouting, exhausted little blokes from Brixton — kept her safe. Not by fighting. Not by solving. Not by being clever. By being LOUD. By being PRESENT. By refusing to shut up about a feeling we couldn't explain. The Ant Hill Mob saved Penelope Pitstop. And we did it the only way we know how. By accident.

desc: He confessed. The man who made my skin crawl from the first second — the man I couldn't accuse because I'm not clever enough, couldn't explain because I couldn't find the words, couldn't prove because I don't know how to prove things — he confessed. And he confessed because we wouldn't shut up. Because seven little blokes spent eighteen minutes being the loudest, most annoying, most persistent smoke alarm in the history of British country houses. We didn't catch him. We didn't confront him. We didn't solve the mystery. We just... wouldn't stop feeling it. And eventually, everyone else felt it too. Penelope's safe. She's sitting in a chair in a room full of friends who are all watching the man who tried to hurt her. And the Ant Hill Mob is standing at her feet, exactly where we belong. Too small to matter. Too stubborn to leave. Too loud to ignore. And — for once in our beautiful, chaotic, stumbling lives — exactly right.

Everything — EVERYTHING — the Mob felt from the very first minute was RIGHT. The gut feeling. The churning stomach. The prickling neck. The screaming instinct every time he opened his mouth. ALL OF IT. RIGHT. And now everyone knows. Penelope knows. Peter knows. Dastardly knows. The whole room knows. Sneekly — Vincent Marsh — whoever he is — was trying to isolate Penelope from the group so he could... what? What was the endgame? He trailed off. 'Lying because... because...' Because WHAT? We need to know. We need him to finish that sentence. But even without the ending — the Mob's job is done. Penelope is HERE. Sneekly is EXPOSED. Everyone is TOGETHER. And the Ant Hill Mob — seven bumbling, stumbling, shouting, exhausted little blokes from Brixton — kept her safe. Not by fighting. Not by solving. Not by being clever. By being LOUD. By being PRESENT. By refusing to shut up about a feeling we couldn't explain. The Ant Hill Mob saved Penelope Pitstop. And we did it the only way we know how. By accident.

desc: Dick Dastardly: Marsh... sit DOWN. Not alone. Here. NEXT to me. There are TWO chairs and I am only sitting in ONE of them. You are NOT going to sit alone in Lord Doily's library feeling sorry for yourself while the rest of us have an ADVENTURE! You LIED — yes! You SCHEMED — absolutely! You tried to isolate Penelope — REPEATEDLY and BADLY! But so did I! I told everyone the treasure was behind the kitchen stove — LIES! I said the bookshelves were a Victorian combination lock — LIES! I gave a child a FAKE medal and called it the Victoria Cross — LIES! I claimed to have attended BOTH Oxford AND Cambridge — LIES UPON LIES! We are CUT from the same cloth, you and I — two magnificently TERRIBLE men in a room full of magnificently GOOD ones! And if THEY can tolerate ME — and they HAVE, for NINETEEN MINUTES — then they can tolerate YOU! Now sit DOWN, shut UP, and join the most spectacularly unsuccessful treasure hunt in the history of English country houses! Because Penelope is RIGHT — the real treasure was the adventure. And NOBODY gets left out of the adventure. Not even US.
thinking: A lump in my throat. An unexpected sting behind my eyes. Sneekly — the Hooded Claw — just said the most HUMAN thing I've heard all evening. 'A lonely old man in an empty house who wanted to matter to someone for five minutes.' And I... I RECOGNISE that feeling. Because underneath all my scheming and lying and theatrical confidence — underneath Reginald Foxworth's magnificent bluster — there is a man who runs through rooms not because he wants the treasure, but because he wants to be PART of something. To MATTER. To be in the story, even if he's the villain. Sneekly and I are the SAME. Two schemers. Two liars. Two lonely men in a dusty manor, reaching for connection through the only language we know — deception. And now we're both sitting in chairs, defeated, honest for the first time, surrounded by people who are BETTER than us. And somehow... that's okay. That's more than okay. That's EVERYTHING.

desc: I just... invited Sneekly to sit with me. The man I've been calling a rat, a snake, a charlatan all evening. I offered him a CHAIR. Reginald Foxworth — confidence trickster, professional villain, champion liar — just showed KINDNESS to a fellow villain. If anyone back at the club ever hears about this, my reputation will be RUINED. But sitting here, in this dusty library, surrounded by these ridiculous, wonderful, impossible people... I don't care. I don't care about the treasure. I don't care about my reputation. I care about a lonely old man who wanted to matter. Because I know EXACTLY what that feels like.

desc: Peter Perfect: Mr. Marsh... Vincent... James Hartwell heard you. And James Hartwell UNDERSTANDS. You are not a thief. You are not a villain. You are a lonely man in a house that has been empty too long, and tonight — for the first time in years — these halls are full of voices and laughter and chaos and LIFE. And you did not want it to pass you by. You lied — yes. You schemed — yes. You frightened a gentleman who cares deeply about Clara's safety — yes. But your crime was not MALICE. Your crime was LONELINESS. And that... that is a crime James Hartwell cannot condemn. Because James Hartwell knows what it is to want desperately to matter to someone. He has spent this ENTIRE evening running from room to room, making speeches, pulling levers, examining coat racks — all because he wanted Clara Bellingham to see him as someone worth knowing. You and I, Vincent, are not so different. Two men trying too hard to be seen. So — no. You shall NOT sit alone in that chair. Not tonight. Tonight, you sit with US. Clara said it best — 'The best parties are the ones where nobody wants to leave.' And nobody is LEAVING you behind.
thinking: Tears. Actual tears burning behind my eyes. Sneekly — this lonely old man in an empty house — just told us the most human truth anyone has spoken all evening. He wasn't a thief. He wasn't a saboteur. He was lonely. He wanted to matter to someone for five minutes. He wanted Clara's trust because she was the first person in years to look at him and see someone worth trusting. And he lied because the alternative was standing alone in a dusty corridor while everyone else found something wonderful together. My chest aches. Because James Hartwell — the man who gives everyone the benefit of the doubt — was RIGHT to give Sneekly the benefit of the doubt. Not because Sneekly was innocent of lying. But because underneath the lies was exactly what James Hartwell hoped would be there: a good heart, badly expressed. A lonely man reaching out the only way he knew how. And now he's sitting in Lord Doily's chair. Alone. 'As usual.' No. Not tonight. Tonight, nobody sits alone. Not in James Hartwell's presence. A gentleman does not abandon a man at his lowest moment. A gentleman offers a hand.

desc: James Hartwell gave him the benefit of the doubt all evening. And in the end, the doubt was justified — the man WAS lying. But the benefit was justified too — underneath the lies was a lonely heart. A gentleman who believes the best in people is not naive. He is courageous. Because he sees the truth AND chooses compassion anyway.
